headline: Clean Energy Super PAC Outspends Trump Loyalists to Sink Anti-Renewable Republican in South Carolina
deck: A $1 million ad blitz by solar-backed donors flipped a key GOP primary, signaling a new power bloc in Republican politics.
body: A clean energy super PAC bankrolled by solar entrepreneurs and Silicon Valley investors just bankrolled the defeat of Rep. Ralph Norman in South Carolina’s Republican Senate primary, handing victory to challenger Darline Graham. The Invest in Tomorrow Coalition (ITC) spent $1 million to paint Norman as a turncoat to both Donald Trump and the renewable energy movement, a strategy that upended the race in Graham’s favor. The outcome marks the second time this year the ITC has deployed its war chest against Norman, who also lost a gubernatorial bid earlier this summer. The group’s intervention underscores the rising influence of clean energy donors in Republican primaries, even when their targets claim conservative credentials.

Norman’s crime, in the eyes of the ITC, was his perceived apostasy on renewable energy. Once a co-founder of the Congressional Solar Caucus in 2018, he spent 2024 trying to distance himself from the group after a $5 million grant went to Silfab Solar for a manufacturing plant in his district. The ITC argued that his shift amounted to betrayal, deploying ads that accused him of being a ‘MAGA traitor’ and asking, ‘Trump doesn’t want him. Why would we?’

The ITC’s messaging was not subtle. Its ads framed Norman’s wavering support for clean energy as a violation of conservative loyalty, a tactic that resonated in a primary where Trump’s endorsement is often a deciding factor. ‘In a Republican primary, a candidate’s fidelity to Trump is one of the most important topics,’ said Tom Matzzie, chief executive of CleanChoice Energy and chair of the ITC. ‘If that is what works, that is what we are going to spend money on.’

Matzzie made clear the group’s long game. While Graham’s victory was the immediate prize, the ITC’s broader goal is to reshape Republican caucus dynamics by demonstrating the political cost of opposing renewable energy. ‘We certainly hope that Darline Graham will appreciate our support and consider it when contemplating her positions on future issues,’ Matzzie told reporters. ‘But what we are trying to do is create chatter amongst members of Congress, that Ralph Norman betrayed the industry and the industry held him accountable for it.’

The ITC’s spending spree is part of a deliberate strategy to weaponize conservative rhetoric against candidates who waver on clean energy. By framing opposition to renewables as disloyalty to Trump’s base, the group is exploiting a vulnerability in GOP primaries where ideological purity often trumps policy pragmatism. Norman’s loss suggests the tactic is working, at least in races where the clean energy sector has a clear financial stake.

The implications extend beyond South Carolina. If the ITC can successfully sway Republican primaries by linking renewable energy opposition to electoral peril, other lawmakers may think twice before aligning with fossil fuel interests. The group’s Silicon Valley and solar industry backers are betting that their dollars can shift the GOP’s center of gravity on energy policy, even if the messaging relies on the same culture-war playbook that has defined Trump-era politics.

For now, the ITC’s victory is a data point in a broader experiment: Can clean energy donors, operating within the GOP’s own rules, force a party historically tied to oil and gas to confront the political realities of a changing energy landscape? The answer may determine whether renewable energy becomes a litmus test—or at least a litmus-tested issue—in future Republican primaries.
